It's three in the morning and you're awake, doing the arithmetic. For most of human history, that wasn't the problem — it was the schedule.

A historian found more than five hundred references to "first sleep" and "second sleep" scattered through old court records, diaries and medical books. Before cheap artificial light, a night in much of Europe came in two pieces, with an hour of quiet wakefulness in the middle. Then a sleep researcher reproduced it in a lab. And then anthropologists found the whole thing might not be universal after all.
